paper_information.title: Major Diseases of Green Gram, Black Gram and Their Integrated Management Strategies
paper_information.abstract_summary: This chapter summarizes an exploration of major diseases affecting green gram and black gram, detailing their causal agents, symptomatology, epidemiology, and integrated disease management (IDM) strategies.
paper_information.research_objective: To serve as a concise guide for stakeholders offering insights into effective disease control measures, fostering sustainable practices, and enhancing the productivity of green gram and black gram.
important_findings: Yellow mosaic disease is caused by four begomoviruses and vectored by Bemisia tabaci, causing yield losses from 10 to 100%.
Cercospora leaf spot causes yield losses of 50-70% and is favored by high temperatures and high relative humidity.
Powdery mildew causes yield losses of 9-50%.
Anthracnose causes yield losses ranging between 24% and 67%.
Urdbean leaf crinkle virus (ULCV) can cause up to 100% yield loss.

diseases.causal_agent: Mungbean yellow mosaic India virus (MYMIV), mungbean yellow mosaic virus (MYMV), horsegram yellow mosaic virus (HgYMV), and dolichos yellow mosaic virus (DoYMV)

general: Small yellow spots or patches on the green lamina of young leaves that develop into golden yellow mosaic or bright yellow mosaic symptoms.
Complete yellowing of the leaves as infection progresses.
Significantly delays plant maturity, decreases flower production, and hampers pod formation.
Severely affected plants produce undersized and immature seeds.
early_symptoms: Small yellow spots or patches on the green lamina of young leaves.
advanced_symptoms: Complete yellowing of leaves, necrotic centre within yellow spots in some varieties, small and distorted pods, and plant death before seed set in severe cases.
visual_field_symptoms: Golden yellow mosaic or bright yellow mosaic patterns on leaves.

field_identification: Observation of small yellow spots/patches on young leaves developing into bright yellow mosaic symptoms.

causes_and_risk_factors: Weed hosts acting as reservoirs such as Croton sparsiflorus, Acalypha indica, Eclipta alba
disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) and through grafting; not transmitted through seed, soil, or sap.
epidemiology: The epidemic is increasing every year in all urdbean and mungbean cultivating areas because of its vector whitefly.
severity_and_yield_loss: Average yield loss varies from 10 to 100%, depending on the stage of infection and genotype.

cultural_management: Crop rotation with non-host plants and maintaining field hygiene by removing infected plant debris.
Adjusting sowing dates and plant population.
Rogueing infected plants up to 45 days.
integrated_management: Vector control using insecticidal sprays, reflective mulches, and yellow sticky traps @ 12 traps per hectare

prevention: Use of disease-free seeds and resistant varieties
farmer_action_points: Install Yellow Sticky Traps @ 12 traps per hectare.
Remove infected plants up to 45 days after sowing.

diseases.causal_agent: Cercospora cruenta and Cercospora canescens Ell. & Martin

general: Numerous small leaf spots with grey centres and reddish-brown margins on leaves, branches, petioles, and pods.
Spots grow larger and lead to defoliation under favorable conditions.
advanced_symptoms: Complete darkening and death of the entire pod, shrivelled and dark seeds within infected pods.
visual_field_symptoms: Leaf spots with grey centres and reddish-brown margins.

field_identification: Water-soaked spots turning into small leaf spots with grey centres and reddish-brown margins.

disease_development_and_spread: Spreads by wind and rain splashing spores from cotyledons or infected debris to other plant parts.

cultural_management: Intercropping with tall-growing cereals and millets and mulching
Removal and destruction of infected plant debris
biological_management: Exploring biocontrol agents such as microbial antagonists or beneficial fungi.

integrated_management: Crop rotation, agronomic practices, sanitation, proper plant spacing, fungicide applications, and host plant resistance.

prevention: Seed treatment with captan or thiram
farmer_action_points: Remove and destroy infected plant debris.
warnings_and_limitations: Rotating different classes of fungicides is essential to prevent resistance development.

general: White powdery patches appear on leaves and other green areas, later becoming dull in colour and covering lower leaf surfaces.
Whitish powdery growth containing conidia and mycelium turning dirty white.
Heavily infected plant parts become distorted and shrivelled, leading to yellowing of foliage and premature defoliation.
early_symptoms: White powdery patches appear on leaves and other green areas.
advanced_symptoms: Complete coverage of leaf surfaces by whitish powdery growth, distorted and shrivelled parts, premature defoliation, and forced premature maturity.
visual_field_symptoms: White to dirty white powdery patches on leaves and stems.

field_identification: Presence of white powdery patches on leaves and green parts.

causes_and_risk_factors: Older plants are more susceptible than young plants.
disease_development_and_spread: Survives as cleistothecia in infected plant debris or as oidial form on alternative hosts like Lathyrus sativa, Vicia faba, Vigna ungulate. Spread by air-borne conidia and rain splash.
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss varies from 9% to 50% in farmers' fields.

cultural_management: Improving air circulation and reducing plant crowding
biological_management: Employing biological control agents such as beneficial fungi or bacteria.

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Effective in controlling the disease under field conditions.

diseases.causal_agent: Colletotrichum truncatum (Schw.) Andrus and Moore (also C. lindemuthianum, C. dematium, and C. graminicola)

general: Circular, black, sunken spots with dark centres and bright red-orange margins on leaves and pods.
Withering of affected plant parts in severe infestations.
Seedling blight if infection occurs just after emergence.
early_symptoms: Circular, black, sunken spots on leaves and pods.
advanced_symptoms: Withering of plant parts and seedling blight.
visual_field_symptoms: Sunken black spots with red-orange margins on leaves and pods.

field_identification: Circular, black, sunken spots with dark centres and bright red-orange margins.

causes_and_risk_factors: Early sowing during June is more susceptible compared to late sowing.

other_conditions: Negative correlation with min/max temperatures, positive correlation with rainfall and RH

disease_development_and_spread: Seed-borne primary infection. Secondary spread via air-borne conidia disseminated by spattering rains and wind currents.

cultural_management: Remove crop debris from the field after harvesting.

chemical_management.timing: Onset of symptoms and repeated 15 days later
Onset of symptoms and repeated 15 days later

integrated_management: Debris removal, hot water seed treatment, resistant varieties, fungicide seed treatment, and foliar sprays.

prevention: Hot water seed treatment at 58°C for 15 minutes.

general: Abnormal enlargement of leaves, curling, crinkling, or rugosity.
Initial symptoms appear on the third trifoliate as light green colour with slight expansion of leaflets and raised inter-venal areas.
Subsequent leaves display malformations, increased size, and crinkled lamina surface up to 1.5 times healthy leaves.
Shortened internodes resulting in clumping of apical growth and bushy inflorescences.
Delayed flowering, malformed small flower buds that fail to open, reduced pollen fertility and pod setting.
early_symptoms: Initial noticeable symptom appears in the third trifoliate, exhibiting a light green colour with slight expansion of leaflets and raised inter-venal areas.
advanced_symptoms: Leaf malformations, crinkled lamina, shortened internodes, bushy inflorescences, and reduced pod setting.
visual_field_symptoms: Crinkled, enlarged leaves with curled margins and clumped apical growth.

field_identification: Leaf crinkling, rugosity, and enlargement starting from the third trifoliate.

causes_and_risk_factors: Presence of weed hosts like Aristolochia bracteata and Digera arvensis
Continuous cropping of other legume crops like cowpea, pigeon pea, taparybean

other_conditions: Kharif season crops are highly susceptible

disease_development_and_spread: Spread via grafting, insect vectors, sap, and seeds (up to 15% in mungbean). Vectors include aphids (Aphis gossypii, A. craccivora), whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), and beetles (Henosepilachna dodecastigma).
severity_and_yield_loss: Up to 100% yield losses depending upon variety and season; complete seed production failure in early-infected plants.

cultural_management: Removing all collateral weed hosts from the field and rouging out infected plants

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Can reduce whitefly populations and the incidence of leaf crinkle.
Reported to reduce the severity of ULCV infection.

integrated_management: Use of disease-free seeds, weed removal and rogueing, hot water treatment, resistant varieties, foliar sprays of insecticides/botanicals, and nutrient application (nitrogen, potash, phosphorus, boron, zinc, and NAA).

prevention: Hot water seed treatment at 52°C for 20–30 minutes
farmer_action_points: Remove collateral weed hosts and rogue out infected plants.
research_findings: Application of nitrogen, potash, phosphorus, boron, zinc, and naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) showed effectiveness in reducing ULCV infection.

paper_level_notes: The paper reviews major diseases affecting green gram and black gram in India, providing comprehensive details on causal agents, symptoms, disease cycles, and integrated management strategies.
